title_en: Saqifah and the Succession of Abu Bakr
title_ar: سقيفة بني ساعدة وبيعة أبي بكر
summary: On the day of the Prophet's ﷺ death, the Ansar gathered at the covered hall of Banu Saida to determine succession. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ؓ, Umar ibn al-Khattab ؓ, and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah ؓ arrived and argued that leadership must remain with the Quraysh. After debate, Abu Bakr was pledged as the first Caliph of Islam. Ali ibn Abi Talib ؓ gave his bayah several weeks later.
narrative:
While Ali ibn Abi Talib ؓ and other close family members were occupied with washing and preparing the Prophet's ﷺ body, a gathering was already underway at the Saqifah Banu Saida — the covered assembly hall of the Banu Saida clan among the Ansar. The Ansar were moving to select one of their own as the new leader of the Muslim community, with Sad ibn Ubadah al-Khazraji as the leading candidate.

Abu Bakr ؓ, Umar ؓ, and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah ؓ learned of the gathering and made their way there immediately. Al-Tabari's account — based primarily on the detailed eyewitness narrative of Umar himself, preserved through Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf — is the most comprehensive classical source for what transpired.

Umar ؓ had intended to speak but Abu Bakr ؓ rose first and delivered a measured, authoritative address. He acknowledged the virtue of the Ansar, their unmatched service to Islam, and their status as the helpers of the faith. He then argued that Arab custom and the nature of the Islamic community required that leadership reside with the Quraysh: 'The Arabs will submit to no one except a man from the Quraysh — they are the central tribe of Arabia and the noblest in genealogy.' He offered the Ansar one of two options: either Umar or Abu Ubaydah. Both declined, saying Abu Bakr was the most worthy.

Among the Ansar, voices arose for a joint leadership: 'A leader from us and a leader from you.' Umar ؓ rejected this as unworkable — two swords in one sheath. Al-Tabari records heated exchange, including a group of the Khazraj who had not accepted the Aws's position and were preparing to pledge to Sad ibn Ubadah. At a critical moment, Umar ؓ seized Abu Bakr's hand and pledged allegiance to him, followed immediately by Abu Ubaydah. The gathering then gave its bayah to Abu Bakr ؓ.

The following day, Abu Bakr ؓ took his place on the mimbar of the mosque and received the formal public bayah of the community. His address defined the nature of the caliphate: 'I have been placed in authority over you, but I am not the best of you. If I do right, support me; if I do wrong, correct me. Truthfulness is a trust and lying is a betrayal. The weak among you shall be strong in my sight until I restore to them their right, God willing; the strong among you shall be weak in my sight until I take from them what is due to others, God willing… Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger; and if I disobey Allah and His Messenger, you owe me no obedience.'

Ibn Kathir records that Ali ibn Abi Talib ؓ — occupied with the burial and deeply grieving — did not immediately join the general bayah. Classical sources differ on the timing of his pledge: Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari both record that it came after the death of Fatimah ؓ approximately six months later. When he did pledge, the relationship between Ali ؓ and Abu Bakr ؓ remained respectful, and Ali ؓ gave no indication of considering the caliphate illegitimate.

The Saqifah decision was the first major political event of the post-prophetic community. It shaped the structure of Islamic governance and became, centuries later, the primary historical reference point for the divergence between Sunni and Shia understanding of succession. Classical Sunni scholarship holds the selection of Abu Bakr as valid through consultation (shura) and the bay'ah; Shia tradition holds that explicit designation of Ali ؓ at Ghadir Khumm was superseded at Saqifah. Both positions draw on events that are historically attested but interpreted through different frameworks of authority.
